base_method_text.title:
Efficient coding of natural scene statistics predicts discrimination
  thresholds for grayscale textures
base_method_text.summary:
Previously, in (Hermundstad et al., 2014), we showed that when sampling is
limiting, the efficient coding principle leads to a "variance is salience"
hypothesis, and that this hypothesis accounts for visual sensitivity to binary
image statistics. Here, using extensive new psychophysical data and image
analysis, we show that this hypothesis accounts for visual sensitivity to a
large set of grayscale image statistics at a striking level of detail, and also
identify the limits of the prediction. We define a 66-dimensional space of
local grayscale light-intensity correlations, and measure the relevance of each
direction to natural scenes. The "variance is salience" hypothesis predicts
that two-point correlations are most salient, and predicts their relative
salience. We tested these predictions in a texture-segregation task using
un-natural, synthetic textures. As predicted, correlations beyond second order
are not salient, and predicted thresholds for over 300 second-order
correlations match psychophysical thresholds closely (median fractional error
<0.13).
base_method_text.main_contributions: The study investigates the relationship between natural scene statistics and visual perception by testing the "variance is salience" hypothesis for grayscale textures. It defines a 66-dimensional space of local grayscale light-intensity correlations and demonstrates that human sensitivity to second-order correlations closely matches predictions derived from natural image statistics. The research also identifies invariances in psychophysical thresholds that reflect symmetries in natural images.
base_method_text.methodology: The methodology involves analyzing natural images to quantify the variance of different grayscale texture correlations. Psychophysical experiments are conducted using a texture-segregation task with synthetic textures. Observers report the location of textured strips, and detection thresholds are measured. The predicted thresholds based on natural image statistics are compared with the psychophysical thresholds.
base_method_text.experimental_setup: The UPenn Natural Image Database and van Hateren database are used for natural image analysis. Synthetic grayscale textures with three luminance levels (black, gray, light) are generated using a Markov process to control the correlations. A four-alternative forced-choice paradigm is used in the psychophysical experiments, and thresholds are determined by fitting a Weibull function to the subject's performance.
base_method_text.limitations: The study acknowledges that the efficient-coding model has limitations, as indicated by systematic discrepancies between natural-image predictions and measured thresholds, particularly underestimation in simple planes and overestimation in mixed planes. The preprocessing pipeline reduces the dark-light asymmetry present in natural images, potentially affecting the results. The model also assumes linearity, which may not fully capture the complexities of visual processing.
base_method_text.future_research_directions: Future research directions include exploring the limits of texture adaptation by considering the cost-benefit trade-offs of efficiently coding increasingly complex environmental statistics. The authors suggest investigating non-linear transformations of natural-image variances to improve the model's accuracy. Generalizing the construction to larger numbers of gray levels and correlations over greater distances is also mentioned.

add_method_texts.title:
Learning High-Frequency Functions Made Easy with Sinusoidal Positional
  Encoding
add_method_texts.summary:
Fourier features based positional encoding (PE) is commonly used in machine
learning tasks that involve learning high-frequency features from
low-dimensional inputs, such as 3D view synthesis and time series regression
with neural tangent kernels. Despite their effectiveness, existing PEs require
manual, empirical adjustment of crucial hyperparameters, specifically the
Fourier features, tailored to each unique task. Further, PEs face challenges in
efficiently learning high-frequency functions, particularly in tasks with
limited data. In this paper, we introduce sinusoidal PE (SPE), designed to
efficiently learn adaptive frequency features closely aligned with the true
underlying function. Our experiments demonstrate that SPE, without
hyperparameter tuning, consistently achieves enhanced fidelity and faster
training across various tasks, including 3D view synthesis, Text-to-Speech
generation, and 1D regression. SPE is implemented as a direct replacement for
existing PEs. Its plug-and-play nature lets numerous tasks easily adopt and
benefit from SPE.
add_method_texts.main_contributions: The paper introduces Sinusoidal Positional Encoding (SPE), a novel positional encoding method that learns adaptive frequency features aligned with the underlying function. It addresses the limitations of existing positional encodings (PEs) that require manual hyperparameter tuning and struggle with learning high-frequency functions, especially with limited data. The key finding is that SPE consistently achieves enhanced fidelity and faster training across various tasks without hyperparameter tuning.
add_method_texts.methodology: SPE augments PE with periodic activation functions, making the number and frequencies of Fourier series trainable and adaptive to inputs. It uses a sinusoidal activation function after the traditional positional encoding to allow the network to learn the optimal frequency features. The method can be implemented as a direct replacement for existing PEs.
add_method_texts.experimental_setup: The paper evaluates SPE on 3D view synthesis (NeRF), Text-to-Speech generation (FastSpeech), and 1D regression with neural tangent kernel (NTK). For NeRF, the Blender dataset is used. Performance is measured using PSNR, SSIM, Wavelet Decomposition Power Ratio (WDPR), and Relative Wasserstein Distance Error (RWDE).
add_method_texts.limitations: The paper does not explicitly discuss limitations of the SPE method itself. However, it implicitly acknowledges that the effectiveness of SPE, like other neural network techniques, depends on the architecture of the MLP and the number of parameters.
add_method_texts.future_research_directions: The paper suggests potential for exploring other periodic activation functions and network architectures to further enhance the performance of SPE. Also, the use of GANs to further refine the results from SPE-enhanced NeRF models are worth further investigation.
